transcript.text: Call the meeting to order. We will start with a roll call in the seating of alternates. I have myself present, Anne Parme present, and Susan England who is an alternate will seat her for the vacancy. And we've got Anne and Kevin, our new alternates to be that just have not made it through the swearing in process. So for purposes of the meeting tonight and the discussion of the regulations and that, you're welcome and encouraged to participate in those discussions. But I can't seat you on the commission to actually vote on anything until we get you sworn in. So happy with that. Moving on to Item three, addition or changes to the agenda. I would like to add one item to the agenda and make that Item 6C under new business, and that would be to approve the budget for next year. And so to get that well, first let me ask, are there any other additions or changes to the agenda that anybody else has?
I have a question. On the agenda, under the Rights Away discussion, is there an address there? I do not have the agenda in front of me.
There An address on the agenda? It is on the agenda, yeah. It's new business 6B.
But is there an address? No, there's no address. No, there is no That's fine. It's fine. There doesn't need to be. Okay. And

I am prepared to put up the picture of the lot if we need that to help out that discussion. So again, the one change to the agenda is Add Item six, Charlie, twenty twenty one-twenty two budget. And I need a motion to add that to the agenda. So Ann or Susan?
I move that we add Item 6C, approval of the budget for fiscal year twenty twenty one to the agenda.
Thank you, Susan. Can I get a second in? Second. Thank you, and Taking a roll call vote, Ann, how do you vote? Aye.

Susan? Aye. And I vote aye as well. Motion carries three zero, zero to add the budget to the new business agenda. I see nobody present from the public. So I guess there'll be no public comment at this point. Moving on to old business. I show new old business. I wrestled with myself whether the Lake Reg should be old business or new business. But I figured we'll let that stay in the new business there. And so we'll move on to item 6A, which is the lake regulations. And I was hoping that Scott would at least be here. He's been having, I know he's pretty interested in that. Not sure why he's not here tonight, but anyhow, we're gonna, we'll go through them and Mindy, if you can allow me to do the screen share, I can call up the regulations and we'll go through those.
All right, you should be able to now enabled screen sharing for everybody.

Okay. Okay, so this is the draft of the proposed lake regs under section two, which is the district's section of our regulations. This would add down here the Andover Lake Watershed Protection overlay zones. Now one of the things I changed from the previous draft was I put a Z on the end of the acronym there. I still don't know how to pronounce it, but that gave the first letter of all the words instead of leaving zones out of that. So that was no big deal, but that includes our overlay zones into the discussion on the different districts there. If we come down under item 2.2, it talks about the zoning map for the town of Andover, which is promulgated at this point, and that shows the whole town and shows where the Lake District is, where the industrial business districts are, that sort of thing. And it says this is included in Appendix one. If you were to go to our website right now, you would see that on the section that has the different documents for us, that's listed as Appendix A. So we're going to need to change that on the website so that it's consistent

with our regulations. So that's pretty straightforward, no big discussion there. The amended map, you would go down and we're talking about the Andover Lake Watershed Protection Map and it says adopted, you can see back we thought we would get this adopted in 2019. Didn't happen there yet and it'll end up being 2021 before we get it adopted but that's the watershed map and for the benefit of Anne and Kevin, let me just see if I can call that up without losing where everything's at there. So that's from the presentation we went through before and talked about the yellow being Zone A along the lake, light blue is Zone B, the purple Zone C, and then the brown is outside the Lake District and that's our Zone D. So anyhow, that's the map. That is not an approved map and so we'd have to get that approved at the public hearing where we go through our different regulations. So that's it on the establishment of the districts. Anybody got any questions on that? And that takes care of the two comments that we've got in there as well.

Moving down into new section 7.6 which is in the section of our regulations on the Andover Lake District and it goes through a bunch of intent for the first section here. There was a comment, I think this was by Hillary, our Liminologist, and she was saying depends on the size of the disturbed land and construction projects, possible deep enforcement. The enforcement we're looking at there is whether or not DEEP would require us to put sewers into Andover, which is very costly and we don't have the money for that right this minute. I think if we can avoid that, that's probably good. That was that comment. Talked about phosphorus and nitrogen transferred directly to the lake by stormwater runoff. Unless the velocity of surface water is reduced. That takes care of one of her next comments. Moving down here, what I've highlighted in yellow are words that I have added to since the version that's currently posted in the pending regulations on our website there. And I tried to put in some words that took care of the next couple of comments here. So comment five is talking about reducing runoff volume and increasing infiltration of green water. I added that in there. We were talking about mitigating increases due to development

and increases in impervious surface. Mitigation measures also help maintain the water table at healthy levels. And I didn't want our regulations to be the technical manual that somebody goes to to figure out how to take care of the lake. And so I put in some words that were specifically commented on but I don't think anybody that lives around the lake or in the Lake District is going to go read our zoning regs to find out how to to maintain the lake healthy. But maybe it's an education process for us. It certainly was me. You know, one of the comments later on, Hillary, you know, suggested that certainly if somebody's building the house or doing a significant upgrade, we ought to encourage them to do extra, above which required mitigation measures. And so the next paragraph here talks about that and talks about Jim being available to help determine the most effective place to mitigate stormwater runoff. So we'd like the property owners to do more than is required and that takes care of that. And then the last one is just a comment I added. I don't know if it would work or not,

but as a property owner on the lake who might be thinking about improving something later on, would somebody be worried about not taking action to mitigate stormwater runoff because then you don't have that to do or get any credit for it the next time you want to improve your property. So I put that in there and that can be a discussion with the zoning agent as well. So that's why I added those couple of things in there. I see the next comment and Jim, if you can mark this down for me just so I remember to go back to it. I see we go right from 7.6.0 to 7.6.2. I didn't notice that before. So I've got to get the numbering system down here. Hilary was asking about the stormwater management plan, is it available? I sent that to her. It is available in our regulations. And she asked who designed the nutrient allocation worksheet and that was something

borrowed from the town of Columbia, modified it a little bit, but that was in there. So that took care of those two comments and I fed that back to Hillary as well. In the requirements section here going down, so it says once implemented all best management practices shall be maintained, kept in working condition by the property owner and such obligations shall be contained in the declaration of covenants and restrictions in accordance with the form contained in Appendix four. My question there was, do we have, well, know we don't have an appendix for it. All we have is appendix one right this minute, but we don't have that form either. And so, you know, I was talking to Jim about that. If we need to keep a record of the mitigation measures if somebody did, we can do that without having this declaration of covenants and restrictions form, which we don't have and I couldn't find anybody who knew anything about that. So I'm just going to go ahead and eliminate that. And again, I'm just rambling through here. If there's any questions on any of these things, please don't hesitate to ask. I'm just trying to go through a couple of the comments that both our attorney and the linologist that we had to take a look at it, go from there.

Now, I'm wondering, Jim, do you know if the agenda on the website had the correct link to get into this? I know I sent out an updated link to everybody here. And I know Linda Derek, who's the head of Alma, Andover Lake Management Association, was planning on joining the meeting tonight. I wouldn't expect her to be here necessarily right off the bat. She might think that it takes us a while to get other things done. I'm just wondering if that's precluding anybody from
Jed, you had sent that email to Amanda as well, correct? I don't responded know.
And said, I believe, thanks for pointing that out. Okay, I didn't know if that came from you Jim or if that came from Amanda. Well, it didn't come from me.
Well, anyway. Okay, Leanne, can you hear me? Yes, I can hear you, Leanne. Yeah. Okay. It just took me fifteen minutes to sign in. Okay.
So I'm not sure what's going on. Well, working our way.

We added one item to the agenda, which is going to be a budget discussion item under new business 6C. And we're working our way through the comments from the the late regulations that that I got there so far. Leanne, did you have problems because of Yes, the

I had problems with the passcode. First, it kept hanging up. You know, the recording didn't give me time to enter the passcode. I tried entering both the passcode and meeting ID, five or six times, and the the recording would hang up on me before I could get through it. So I had just kept trying until I got a different screen. But I still can't see all of you. Normally I can, but at least I can hear you and you can hear me. Okay. I don't know why it was so abrupt.
And that probably means so then you're not able to see the regulations as we go through them. And I'll just have to make sure that I'm vocalizing the comments and that sort of thing. Am I seated?
I will seat you as of sevennineteen. So yes, you are seated.
Okay. I'll keep trying to get in where I can see everybody. You can never see me, but I'll keep trying to get to that part. Very good.

Chad, I just had a question before you move on. Yep. So it says Appendix four. I know up above we changed Appendix one because it's referenced as Appendix A on the website. Is Appendix four going to be Appendix B on the website?

No. So there is not going to be an appendix four. I can't find anybody who knows what this form is. You know, it's not something that we had or had been using for other things. And so we will just put a list of the mitigation factors in the building file for the particular home. So what I expect, and let me just cover the appendices for a minute. So we had appendix one was going to be or is by our current regulations, the Andover zoning district map. Appendix two is going to be the watershed overlay zone map. Appendix three was going to be the nutrient allocation worksheet. And what I would like to do is, my intention is not to have the nutrient allocation worksheet be an actual part of the regulations. That is just a tool that we have available to us to help us implement the regulations and it's going to be something that Jim as a zoning agent is using. So I got rid of the reference to appendix three that talked about it. And that gives us the

ability to, as we see process improvements with using that worksheet, I can change those without having to go back to public hearing because it's helping us easily implement the regulations. Doesn't have anything to do with actually defining the regulations or anything like that. So there'll be an appendix one and appendix two and that's all there is there. Okay, yep, so now we're down to and we're still really just providing the basic framework for what these regulations are all about. In 7.6.4, I added some words in here based on our discussion at the last meeting. When an undeveloped lot is developed, it would be very difficult for the property owner to reduce nutrient allocation runoff to achieve the required reduction required by the nutrient allocation worksheet. In this case, at a minimum, the property owner will mitigate stormwater runoff by capturing all roof and driveway runoff in a dry well or detention basin. And I wrestled with myself on this a little bit. Do I need to keep the words driveway or dry well or detention basin or just leave that up to Jim? Jim, you can weigh in on that a little bit. We also talked about giving some allowances for roof, driveway, and lawn. And I went through a case study on just a basic lot. I said, well, just doing the roof and the driveway isn't going to be enough because most of the runoff into the lake comes from the lawn. It runs off doesn't absorb in the lawn and that sort of thing. So I didn't like Scott's recommendation last time. And then we went to the last inland wetlands meeting, we had a potential property owner. I think they're going to buy one of the lots that's

for sale on Lake Road. And they were going to the Wetlands Commission with their plan. So I mentioned to them it'd be nice if they captured all the roof and driveway runoff. And they said, well, the backside of the roof runs towards the road away from the lake and so does the driveway. And so they weren't enamored with just doing this much. I think the thought will grow on them. It just caught them by surprise. But what they did do is they had a very small lawn on that two acre lot. And so in keeping with spirit of the regulations, I thought they did a great job there. I asked Jim, is the guy who's going to have to go work with the property owners and enforce this,

which would you prefer? And he said he's happy with just mitigating the roof and driveway runoff and he is not a big fan of big yards and the couple remaining lots on the lake, I think are well suited to have very small yards around the house here. So I will go with Scott's recommendation, barring any pushback from anybody here.

I do have one comment. Last sentence there in paragraph. We use the term drywall or detention basin. I'm wondering if we couldn't just use storage capacity. Two reasons. One is it would leave the applicant open to use any other means, meaning like a rain garden or whatever. Yep. Which is also allowed elsewhere. And dry wealth to me is not a very clear word. I don't think it's clearly defined. It's used differently by different folks or it has been over the years. I don't think it has a real specific definition from an engineering
point of view. So if I, you said storage capacity? That's what I'm thinking, yeah. Okay, and so there it is. Water storage capacity, perhaps.

Okay, so you like that? Yes, I do. Okay, very good. So that's what that will be. Thank you. In the next paragraph I just added, all that does is that references us down to a section later on where it talks about if you can't comply with the nutrient allocation worksheet, you can submit a special permit and take that to the Planning and Zoning Commission. So I put that in here because it seemed to be a good spot to get that thought in our instructions as we go through there. So that's that and it doesn't really change the content any. Leanne, are you able to see us yet or are you still flying blind?
No, I've done this at least eight times and I'm putting in the passcode. I've checked your email to us today. I've checked the one on the town website and it just says it's wrong. It's 331889.
331889. Yep, that's the passcode. At least that's the one I used to get in.
I don't know what else to do unless I go out and smoke again. I just try the phone, Leanne? Just try what?

I was gonna say the phone, but then you don't have the visual, never mind. Yep. So I think we're doing as good as we can there at this point. Yeah. Jed, I have another comment. Yep. The property owner can submit a special permit. It's really semantics, but I mean, submit an application or apply for a special permit. Submit an application for a special permit. This is

There we go. That one's done deal. Okay. Thank you. Now we get down to where we're actually talking about the regulations in the overlay zone. And so of the, So we're expecting a 10% reduction in nutrients running off into the lake when all is said and done. And then we throw additionally the site plan must demonstrate that it will infiltrate the first two inch flush of storm water or volume of two inch rain event. So that's on top of that 10% reduction. And I said, well, maybe we're asking for too much. And then I said to myself, well, one of the feedback things I did get from Hillary was she thought she was hoping that we would have used a little more technically refined and accurate reduction technique. She thought it was overly simplified. And I agree that it is overly simplified, but we probably need to keep it simple because even then, it takes a while to get the handle of it. And I didn't want to make it too difficult.

But one of the things that certainly comes into play is our regulations do not account for the slope of the property running down into the lake. And a lot of the property has some very significant slopes and so all the water is gonna run off into the lake. Very little has a chance to soak in unless we do something there. So anyhow, I decided that my recommendation is we're going leave that extra two inch flush in there. If it gets to be too cumbersome and everybody's saying they can't do it, then we'll have to look at modifying the regulations. But I think we should try to go with a little bit more and see how we do there. This is where Hillary made the comment, if the homeowners went through the trouble of hiring someone to create best management practices to infiltrate this water, they should be encouraged to infiltrate runoff from existing structures. And I agreed and that's why I put that comment early on in the intent about doing that. But this is where the actual 10% reduction for zone A is our requirement with the two inch flush for the additional impervious sections. And so after that, I'm gonna go down to Zone B, which is the same as Zone A with the exception of instead of a 100 square feet increase, it would be greater than 200 square feet. So we're a little further away from the lake, a little less restrictive, and instead of a 10% reduction, we're looking at a 7.5%

reduction on the nutrient runoff. Then we still have that two inch infiltration of water. Zone C, very similar. Instead of 100 or 200, now it's 300 square feet. Instead of 10 or 7.5%, now it's down to a five, we're expecting a 5% reduction. So that's what all this goes through. Then we get into overlay zone D. And you don't have to do the nutrient allocation worksheet. We're just going to look for a mitigation of that two inch flush of storm water off the newly impervious surfaces. Modifications to the nutrient allocation worksheet. So this just says that if you're doing something and we don't have on our worksheet a coefficient for that improvement to reduce the runoff, you can have your engineer propose one. Jim agrees to it, we can use it, we might include it on our list. But if you recall last time when we were going through, I think we took, we were talking about how did we get the reduction coefficient when we took roof to a dry well. And if I had taken roof to lawn, it would be you take the runoff for roof, which I think is one point zero, and then lawn, which is 0.3, and you'd get the reduction of 0.7. That's how that worked and that's how it should have worked. There wasn't any reduction for a dry well. I think it could have been zero. But there were things on there we didn't have coefficients for.

And so I think by good engineering practice, they were developed over in Columbia and we just continued to use those here. Mitigation of one time small surface change in the A, B and C districts. And again, if you're less than 100 square feet in zone A, 200 square feet in zone B, 300 square feet in zone C, You can put a trench under the roofline and capture the rain and you don't have to go through the process of nutrient allocation worksheet and all that. There was some thought and I think that the thought has some merit. If you're digging a big trench in the Wetland review area, are there times where you would be doing more harm than good by digging this trench in the wetlands area? And that could be. And if Jim is the zoning agent and Joe is the wetlands agent. We're to conclude that that was the case. They can come to us and say we really think it's best if we don't do that for this small improvement. Not worth doing. But I did like having the basic trench or the stone pad, know, preventment under a shed or that kind of thing and we'll keep that in there.

And I talked, once again, we talk about recording in the property records, the form contained in Appendix four, that covenants and restrictions form, which we don't have, and I'm just going to go ahead and eliminate that. Now we get into a section that talks about the best management practice for reduction of nitrogen, and that's just good things to do. Again, don't think anybody's going to be looking in our regs to figure out how to do that. It could happen, it gives us ideas of things that we can talk to the property owner about when he's coming to us for an application and say, could you consider doing some of these things here? Down here, we had something maintain a mulched area, especially on the downslope of lawns and hard surfaces, especially at the edge above the shoreline. I thought, okay, I can do that. But I'm not sure if you put the mulch in there, does that add nutrient to the lake? I used to have a leaf pile down by the shore and I dumped all my leaves there in the fall. And I stopped doing that because I thought that would increase the nutrient running off into the lake. It certainly prevents the water running off into the lake because it gets absorbed into the leaf pile. But based on that's what we had, I left it there and I'll still count on my ability to get smarter as we go along and figure out best how to take care of the lake. Not an expert on that yet. But that was the question on this. It also talks about planting shrubs along the lake, and I think that's a good thing to do too.

Okay, so this is just modification of lake watershed protection requirements by special permit. And this is where it talks about and Jim, see if we got the words that you like here in a case where unable to comply. Okay, so it sort of avoids the issue. It just says the Commission may modify the requirements by special permit. So I guess that's fine with the way that's worded there. And that's what I tied back to that earlier process just so that you knew as you were looking through the regs if there was a problem and you couldn't meet it, we had an out for you on how to go. This is a comment by our attorney. As we write our regulations using the word exemption is no longer in vogue, I guess. And you got to put the restrictions, the specific restrictions. It can't be that the commission can do whatever they want and go implement something. We just can't grant an exemption. We have to have conditions specified so that we're fair across the board with everybody who might be into that condition.

So he says we'll have to keep an eye on this. And so I didn't think that that meant we had to change it right now and I didn't see the word exemption in there. I did use the word exemption, we did, later on, and he didn't have a comment on that, and so I left that for now too. And this just talks about so called first flush infiltration system either has been employed to the max extent possible or not possible as determined by the Commission. And this talks about some soil things we'd have to get help from Jim and the wetlands on when that's not possible. I certainly don't have the technical ability to make that determination. I can see you now. Okay, great. What was the trick, Leanne? I don't remember. Tried so Yeah, many

I've been there, I know how that goes. It happens when I'm working with the TV all the time. You do that. I don't know. It just did. And this talks about what we do do should be attached to the building zoning permit applications filed on land records. And again, nice to have a record of that. We don't have that appendix four form, but there we go. The next demonstration, that property is not within the Andover Lake Watershed. We talked about if somebody is doing a modification and it's not within the watershed, even though he's in Zone D, get he to the zoning agent, they can agree on that and make that determination that he doesn't have to do that. The attorney's comment was that is a decision, We need to make that formally. The zoning agent can still do that, but we need to publish it in case somebody wants to appeal that. But we need to be very formal in our process, we just can't go out there take a look and say yep, looks good to me and we're on our merry way. So that's the caution that we've got to take there. More voluntary actions on what to do with the watershed protection area. And this one's got to do with okay, Jim, I got so here's the second comment for you to do that didn't strike out at me. The initial draft we were looking at had all the voluntary actions in one paragraph. I wanted to split those out and I did split them out, I just didn't move 7.6.14 down into 7.7.

So these are all the things that we can do to improve our septic system in the leach field, but it just needs to be in the septic system in the leach field section of the regulations. So I'll cut and paste and move those down here under 7.7. But that was all the comments that pertained to the rainwater stormwater runoff into the lake. And at this point, so I'd ask the folks who are listening to me babble on, is this a helpful way to go through the regulations or is there a better way? How can we make this a more meaningful process to you folks who are doing the listening? What am I not doing well? This is the first time I've gone through reviewing regulations. I know we had worked hand in hand as a commission in the past on the regulation development. I thought that was too cumbersome for everybody. Tried to make that a little simpler. Anyhow, any feedback before I get into the septic stuff on the regulations?

Jay, I just want to comment on the use of wood chips. It's been pointed out on a number of occasions on recent wetlands walks that a lot of these chips are either non native or died. Perhaps we'd like to look into that a little further and insert the word approved wood chips or something of that nature.
Yep, and do you have a section that that's referring to where it goes talking about the wood chips? I don't offhand, but

I'll find it. Okay, yep. So yeah, make that the third comment that you'll email her after we're done so I can make sure that I get this updated right. Okay, so anyhow, now we're talking about the subsurface discharge. We know we've got a lot of small lots, we've got some old septic systems, and we know that there are some failing septic systems around the lake. So we're trying to figure out what to do to get that really, didn't have any teeth on that. The Eastern Highlands Health District regulates that. And unless you're going in to build something, they don't get involved too much with it. But we wanted to improve the septic systems and there's a lot of folks who thought that would be where we would get the best bang for our buck there. And so, Hilary had made the comment to me, you know, seven point seven point two point one was conditions requiring a new septic system. She said, well, can't you upgrade your existing septic system so that it's fully functional?

And I think that, yeah, you probably can. That sounds like a reasonable thought. You shouldn't have to tear everything out to put it all in to get there. And if there's a professional engineering plan that the health district signs off on, that's fine with me. So anyhow, we said you would put in a new or upgraded system unless and here's where we use that word exemption, and I didn't get any legal pushback on that. And maybe it's because we do have the existing restrictions in here. But the cases for not having to do any improvements to your septic system, and these are probably the most important thing in the whole article,

was we want your leach field to be greater than 18 inches above the max high groundwater table. The initial the earlier drafts that we had talked about this, it was 12 inches, the state or the health district requires 18 and I thought that we should want that too. We're trying to protect the lake, let's increase that distance to whatever the rate requirement is. So I did, I changed that from 12 to 18. Then we had, dependent upon what version you looked at, it said that the septic system leach field had to be, one version said 35 feet from the lake, another version said 50 feet from the lake. Feedback I got from the health district was that they would like to have it 50 feet from the lake,

but on some of the smaller lots along the lake, they reduced that down to 25 feet. And so I couldn't figure out a way to put the right distance in there. You know, 35 didn't sound right, 50 didn't sound right either. And I didn't want to put 25 in there because then when we could get further away, we wouldn't. So I just changed it to exceeds the Eastern Highland Health District distance requirements from high watermark. And so we'll look at that on a case by case basis, but the guy who's having a professional engineer certified that his on-site septic system's good enough, he's going to have to explain to us why whatever distance it is, is correct. And that goes back to, know, a lot right down the street from me here, 294 Lake Road, they just put in a septic system and it was the state who asked us to allow it 21 feet from the lake. I went back looking through that application trying to figure out what that was based on and I couldn't figure out why it was. But if you got a failed septic system, and then you're putting in a new one in the health district and the state both agree with it, who am I to say that that's not an improvement? And so I said, well, just leave the words there fairly nebulous. The third one, as I mentioned, I didn't understand well why we're only asking for exceeds 50%

of the size requirement for a new system. But I went back to the Connecticut state statutes and that's what they have, and so I left it there. And they also said it doesn't meet the technical definition of failing. And then here's some extra credit words that we don't want a professional engineer to just go out there and look at the ground and say, looks good. We're putting some conditions by which he must do the inspection on the septic system to make sure that it's meeting the requirements we're looking for. So I added those words to that since what we posted online is the draft version there. Overlay B is the same. God bless you, whoever that was. We allow the numbers to be a little bit different here on increasing square footage and net floor area and that sort of thing. And so it's a little less restrictive but the requirements for the septic system are the same. We're further away from the lake, so nobody should have to go into that 25 foot requirement rule. So I left the 50 foot thing in for the Zone B. And that's all there is for the septic stuff. We had talked last time about definitions.

I did add some definitions to the definition section of the regulation based on what we were talking. This is not a perfect product here. I took these, I went to Google and tried to get the definitions there, putting these in. And then I went back and looked in our stormwater management plan from our regulations and they have a handful of definitions too. And some of these words aren't exactly matching that there. I don't know if these are better or worse. One of the things that's probably not the greatest in our regulations is I think that we have a section in our regulations on definitions and then each subsection has its own definition thing. So I'll be trying to give some

thought on where the extra definitions can come. This references the other places that some definitions. And that's not all inclusive.
